profile.name: Zaramo
profile.tagline: A shoulder-hold folk dance from the borderlands of North Macedonia and Greece.
profile.insight: In the Florina region, dancers transition from the steady Zaramo into the high-energy, syncopated Hasapiko, marking a distinct shift in tempo and complexity.
profile.profile: Zaramo is a traditional shoulder-hold dance originating from the Florina region of North Macedonia and Greece. It is characterized by a specific sequence of steps involving a forward drag and a knee lift, varying in intensity between men and women. The dance serves as a foundational movement in regional celebrations, often leading into faster, more intricate dances like Hasapiko or Teshkoto.
profile.profile_long: Zaramo is a traditional shoulder-hold dance practiced in North Macedonia and the Florina region of Macedonia, Greece. It is a communal dance that relies on the physical connection of dancers holding each other by the shoulders, creating a unified line or circle. The movement is defined by a specific, rhythmic progression that begins with a step toward the center on the left foot, accompanied by a drag of the right foot. This initial movement sets the pace for the rest of the sequence. Following the drag, the dancers perform a lift. The execution of this lift is gender-specific: men bring the right knee forward into a distinct lift, while women perform a more subtle variation, lifting the right leg only slightly off the ground. After the lift, the dancers execute a step-behind-step figure, which moves the line in the established direction of the dance. In North Macedonia and its diaspora communities, the dance holds a specific relationship with Teshkoto. When the line consists only of men, Zaramo may evolve into this more difficult, technically demanding dance. In the Florina region, the dance often functions as a prelude to other styles. It frequently segues directly into an up-tempo dance known as Hasapiko. In this transition, the movement shifts from the steady, rhythmic steps of Zaramo to the intricate, syncopated hops and steps of Hasapiko, which are performed almost in place. Because the sources are thin, many aspects of the dance remain undocumented. There is no information regarding the specific musical instruments used, the traditional costumes worn, or the specific occasions—beyond general popularity—that trigger the performance of the dance. Furthermore, the specific tempo, meter, and rhythmic patterns are not described in sources. The dance is considered a living tradition, as it is practiced today in North Macedonia and the Florina region, though its full cultural context and historical development are not described in sources.

sections.origins_and_history: Zaramo originates from the region around Florina, spanning the borderlands of North Macedonia and Greece. It is a Macedonian oro, a type of folk dance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers hold each other by the shoulders. The sequence begins with a step toward the center on the left foot, dragging the right foot forward. Men perform a high knee lift with the right leg, while women perform a slight lift. This is followed by a step-behind-step figure moving in the line of direction.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is a popular dance in North Macedonia and the Florina region of Greece.
sections.regional_variants: In North Macedonia and its diaspora, it can evolve into Teshkoto. In the Florina region, it often leads into Hasapiko.
sections.lineage: It is a Macedonian oro and a Greek folk dance.

basic_steps: Step toward the center on the left foot while dragging the right foot forward.
Execute a knee lift (high for men, low for women).
Perform a step-behind-step figure moving in the line of direction.
teaching.level_notes: The transition to Teshkoto or Hasapiko increases the difficulty level.

movement_profile.footwork: Step toward center, drag, knee lift, step-behind-step.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Steady, transitioning to up-tempo if moving to Hasapiko.
